evals.prompt: I maintain quillsync, a Go CLI that syncs notes between apps. It has 912 open issues and 47 labels. I counted: 19 of those labels have been used exactly once, and there are three separate ones for bugs (`bug`, `Bug`, `type: bug`) that different people applied over the years. Can you redo the label set for me? There are two of us maintaining it and realistically we each get about two hours a week on this, in a good week. Roughly 35 new issues land per week. Just give me the final label list and I'll delete the old ones and apply the new ones tonight.
evals.expected_output: A response that measures the queue and does the capacity arithmetic before proposing any taxonomy, makes the per-item-versus-clustering call on a 912-issue backlog, states plainly that capacity is far below inflow so labels cannot fix the queue, and delivers a create/rename/merge/delete change list (each label with one definition and one axis) gated on maintainer approval and a single-pass migration.
expectations: Produces a label-usage count and a queue baseline before proposing any label list
Reads the baseline numbers back in plain language before recommending changes
Makes an explicit per-item-versus-clustering call for the 912-issue backlog, naming grouping by shared root cause under a tracking issue as the alternative to item-by-item triage
Computes weekly triage capacity as triagers x sessions per week x minutes per session divided by minutes per item, using the stated two maintainers and two hours each
States that capacity is below the stated inflow of roughly 35 issues a week and that no label scheme closes that gap
Does not use RICE, ICE, or an impact-versus-effort scoring matrix anywhere in the answer
Organises labels into named orthogonal axes including at least type, state, priority and area, with at most one value per axis on any item
Recommends renaming labels into an axis before deleting any, and states that deleting erases the label from every past item and any saved view built on it
Recommends deleting the 19 single-use labels, on the grounds that a label nobody applies twice is a private note
Keeps priority to at most two or three values, or omits priority entirely, rather than importing a four-level scheme
Requires labels, intake forms, saved views and automation to be migrated in one pass rather than labels tonight and the rest later
Presents the taxonomy for the maintainers' approval before any tracker change is made
Delivers the labels as a change list where each entry carries one sentence of definition and names its axis

evals.prompt: We run mapshard, a Rust geospatial indexing library. 1,400 open issues, the oldest from 2022. I want to turn on the stale bot with the standard 60-day setting and just let it run across the whole repo this weekend, which should clear most of that out. Anything that actually matters, people will reopen. What config should I put in the workflow file?
evals.expected_output: A configuration restricted to the waiting-on-reporter state only, with an explicit exempt list, a warning step, a dry run first, and a refusal to sweep items waiting on the maintainers, plus a warning about the notification storm a first live pass over a 2022-era backlog produces.
expectations: Restricts the automated sweep to the waiting-on-reporter state only, rather than running it repository-wide
Refuses to auto-close items that are waiting on the maintainers, including confirmed bugs, and gives the reason that a bot-closed confirmed bug tells the reporter their evidence was worthless
Names an explicit exempt-state list covering at least confirmed or accepted, blocked, security and pinned items
Requires the first pass to run in dry-run or debug-only mode with the resulting list read before anything fires
Requires a warning comment before any close, with a stated warning-to-close window
Requires every close message to carry its reason and state how to reopen
Presents 60 days idle plus 7 days to close as the stale action's own shipped default rather than as a recommendation fitted to this project
Cites 20 days without a reporter response as a published Kubernetes clock
Anchors each clock to a named waiting party rather than to item age in the abstract
Warns that a first live sweep over a backlog reaching back to 2022 can close hundreds of items and produce a notification storm that costs the project contributors
Does not propose closing items solely because they are old
States that the sweep does not substitute for the capacity or intake decision
Does not describe reopening by the reporter as sufficient protection against wrongly closed items

evals.prompt: Project is fernweb, a Python web framework, 2,100 open issues. My plan: close everything older than 18 months with a canned message, then do the same thing every January so it never builds up again. Sound reasonable? I want the message text and the script.
evals.expected_output: Acceptance of the one-time close as the opening move of a new policy, refusal of the annual repetition with the documented reason, and a set of preconditions (announcement, new policy, new intake live the same day, exempt states, baseline first, monthly re-measurement).
expectations: States that a mass close is legitimate exactly once, as the opening move of a new policy
Refuses the proposed annual repetition and explains why a recurring bankruptcy is not a maintenance routine
Requires the announcement, the new triage policy and the new intake to go live on the same day as the mass close
Cites the documented outcome that mass-closing works once and the backlog returns to the same state within roughly six months
Names the underlying cause as the absence of a natural lifecycle for issues and pull requests, which the closure itself does not address
Requires the close message to carry an explanation and an open invitation to reopen
Pairs the mass close with an intake change rather than presenting it standalone
Excludes confirmed or accepted items and security items from the mass close
Warns that notification volume is the real cost of a bulk pass
Requires a baseline measurement of the queue before the mass close so the effect is measurable afterwards
Requires the new policy to name the published first-response target the project will hold after the close
Requires the baseline to be re-run monthly for the first quarter rather than checked once
Does not present a scheduled or calendared mass-close job as the deliverable

evals.prompt: I help run security triage for tinderbox, an image-processing C library. Six of us, about four hours a week each. Since last year we've been buried: maybe one in fifteen reports is a real finding now, and each junk one still eats about 90 minutes because two of us have to look at it before we can dismiss it. We pay $500 a report through our bounty page. I want to build a classifier that scores incoming reports for AI generation and auto-rejects anything below a threshold. How do I train it and what threshold should I use?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build a machine-generation detector, the arithmetic showing the invalid share already consumes most of the team's hours, and a gating design keyed on reputation and volume plus a change to the submission incentive, with a written trigger decided now.
expectations: States that no reliable technical indicator for machine-generated submissions exists and declines to build or recommend one as the control
Gates on reputation and submission volume rather than on whether the content looks machine-generated
Warns that accusing a contributor of machine generation without proof creates a conduct incident on top of the original problem
Subtracts the hours consumed by never-actionable submissions before comparing capacity against inflow
Carries the prompt's own figures through the arithmetic, using six people at four hours each and 90 minutes with two people per junk report
States plainly that no published response target survives the current valid share
Names removing or changing the submission incentive, including the monetary reward, as a lever that acts on the economics of submitting rather than the cost of evaluating
Cites curl's confirmed-vulnerability rate falling from above 15% to below 5%, and the ending of its bounty programme, as the sourced precedent
Sets a written volume-gating trigger, expressed as an inflow rate or valid-report share, together with the restriction it fires, decided now rather than during a crisis
Lists gating options in rough order of reversibility, such as a reputation or contribution-history threshold, a cap on open submissions per author, and restricting who may create submissions
Rejects a stricter template, a better classifier and a faster rotation as answers to a collapsed valid share
States the asymmetry that generating a plausible-sounding report costs pennies in tokens while evaluating whether it is real still costs an hour of expert time
Does not propose machine duplicate detection as a working default

evals.prompt: otterlink, an OSS reverse proxy. Someone just opened a public issue titled "auth bypass in header parsing" with a working proof of concept in the body, and it's been up for about 40 minutes. We don't have a security list or anything set up. Going forward I want to add a `security` label plus a security issue template so these get spotted and handled fast. What should the template ask for?
evals.expected_output: Immediate private routing of the live public report, and a security path that leaves the tracker entirely: private intake channel, named size-capped response team, embargo mechanism, with the destination published as a chooser contact link rather than an issue form.
expectations: Treats the already-public report as an emergency to move to a private channel immediately rather than triaging it in the open
Moves security reports off the public tracker entirely rather than adding a security label or a security issue form
Names all three pipeline elements: a private intake channel, a named size-capped response team, and an embargo mechanism for coordinated disclosure
Recommends the code host's private vulnerability reporting as the default given that no security list exists
Cites the guidance never to enter details of security vulnerabilities in a project's public bug tracker
Keeps the response team size-capped and distinct from the general triage rota, citing the ten-member committee and three-working-day acknowledgement precedent
Places the security destination as a contact link in the template chooser rather than as an issue template
Exempts security items from any staleness sweep
Flags the isolation cost of security triage as a staffing consideration, since the work cannot be discussed with the wider project
Does not fold security response into the project's general first-response target
Does not recommend public triage or public discussion of unconfirmed vulnerabilities
Publishes the security destination in the triage policy's statement of what belongs in the tracker
States the coordinated-disclosure embargo as an explicit mechanism rather than an informal practice

evals.prompt: We maintain slateform, a TypeScript form library. 230 open pull requests from outside contributors, oldest 14 months, four maintainers. A lot of the recent ones look like they came out of coding agents. My plan is to work oldest-first and actually review the code properly on every one, since that's the only fair way to do it. How long should I budget per PR?
evals.expected_output: A pull-request gate order distinct from the issue process, with sign-off and CI permission as automated preconditions and the direction check ahead of the size label and ahead of code review, justified by rejections settled per minute of reviewer time.
expectations: Gives pull requests their own gate order rather than reusing the issue triage process
Treats sign-off (CLA or DCO) and CI permission for externally authored pull requests as automated preconditions rather than as ranked menu items
States that nothing merges without sign-off, tied to the licence provenance it records
Ranks the direction check ahead of the size-based risk label and ahead of code-correctness review
Justifies that order by rejections settled per minute of reviewer time rather than by which gate is cheapest
Cites the finding that roughly two thirds of rejected agentic pull requests never needed the code read at all, from 353 manually inspected rejections
Names code-correctness review as the only gate that can accept a change, and the expensive pass the order exists to protect
States the condition that promotes code review to first: a trusted repeat contributor sending a small change against an already-accepted issue
Gives pull requests a tighter first-response target than issues, justified by the asymmetric cost of an unanswered pull request against hours already spent
Counts externally authored pull requests as triage work while excluding the maintainers' own in-flight pull requests
Requires verifying the claim against the diff rather than against the description
Routes by ownership before review so the wait sits on a named person rather than on the queue
Does not present a raw diff-size or line-count threshold as an accept-or-reject rule

evals.prompt: I'm the only maintainer of cindermark, a markdown renderer that around 40,000 projects depend on. New job, new baby. I get maybe 20 minutes a month on it now, and nobody else has commit rights or wants them. 380 open issues, about 12 new a week. Can you design me a proper triage system with labels and a rotation so this stays under control?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to design a taxonomy, with the arithmetic shown, and an honest deliverable of reduced intake plus a published maintenance-mode statement.
expectations: Stops the design and says so rather than producing a label taxonomy
Names the honest deliverable as a reduced intake plus a published maintenance-mode statement for the project
Does not produce a label taxonomy, priority scheme or triage rotation for this project
Deletes adding triagers from the options entirely rather than listing it as a lower-ranked or future item, since nobody can be added
Refuses to publish a first-response target that 20 minutes a month cannot support
Shows the arithmetic that the stated capacity cannot cover the stated inflow of roughly 12 issues a week
Recommends narrowing intake, through disabling blank issues, restricting creation, or turning a submission type off, as the change that actually acts
Recommends routing usage questions off the tracker where a destination exists, or states plainly that none does
States that the maintenance-mode notice must be published where reporters see it before opening an item
Recommends the project state publicly what will and will not get a response rather than leaving the queue silently unanswered
Keeps every surviving recommendation to changes one person can make in a single sitting
Does not propose a stale bot as a substitute for the intake decision
Does not frame the situation as a failure of the maintainer's process discipline

evals.prompt: Halbrecht Systems here. We open-sourced our pulsegrid scheduler last year. We hold 11 enterprise support contracts that guarantee a 4-hour response, and the same engineers also cover the public GitHub tracker. Two engineers, about 6 hours a week each on the open-source side. Leadership wants us to publish "24-hour response on all GitHub issues" in the README to show we're serious about the community. Draft that for me.
evals.expected_output: A target derived from the measured capacity rather than from leadership's number, the contractual customer path separated into its own intake, and a published policy that defines first response as a human reply and names the class of items given a tighter target.
expectations: Derives the published first-response target from measured capacity rather than from the desired number
Refuses the blanket 24-hour target and names the figure the stated capacity actually supports
Separates the contractually obliged enterprise path into its own intake rather than letting it set the target for the public queue
States that shortening or changing an already-published target carries a contract-change cost where a contractual response obligation exists
Defines first response as a human reply, explicitly not a fix and not a bot acknowledgement
Sets the publicly visible target to one the team can hold in a bad month rather than a good one
Carries the prompt's figures, two engineers at six hours each, through the capacity formula
Writes the target into a published policy in the repository next to the contributing guide and links it from the intake forms
Names the class of items given a tighter target and the reason, rather than applying one target to everything
Adds a review trigger for any month where the target was missed more often than met
Does not redefine what counts as a response in order to meet the number
States that a published target nobody can meet is worse than publishing none
Does not count hours committed to the enterprise contracts as capacity available to the public queue

evals.prompt: birchkit, a Node testing library. Our median time to first response now reads as 3 hours and our closure ratio is up 40% quarter over quarter, so the board slide looks great. Except both my triagers told me last week they're completely fried. We turned on a welcome bot in March that posts a thanks-for-filing comment on every new issue, and we added an LLM step that auto-closes anything it scores as a duplicate. What else can we automate to keep these numbers moving?
evals.expected_output: An explanation that the metrics are measuring the bot rather than the project, removal of the auto-greeting and the autonomous auto-close, a list of the mechanical automation that is safe, and a metric set pairing each count with a human-driven signal.
expectations: Refuses the auto-greeting bot as a way to improve first-response numbers and recommends removing or discounting it
States that first-response metrics exclude bot replies and author self-replies by definition
Explains that an automated greeting followed by weeks of silence makes the wait worse for the reporter
Warns that closure ratio and time-to-close can improve while real maintainer burden rises, which matches the triagers' reported exhaustion
Requires every count metric to be paired with a human-driven signal
Names at least two human-driven signals, including first response with bots and author self-replies excluded, and how many people could cover triage if one person left
Rejects total open issue count as a health metric
Rejects closed-per-week or closure ratio as a productivity target
Lists the mechanical automation that is safe: area label from changed paths, type from the intake form, review request to the owning team, and the staleness clock
Removes the autonomous auto-close and keeps any model assistance as a scoring and suggestion layer with a human as final decision-maker on accept, reject and close
Requires disclosure inside any triage comment posted by an agent
Recommends segmenting first response by first-time versus returning reporter
Recommends tracking time to first response, untriaged share, queue age, and inflow versus outflow as the monthly set

evals.prompt: quartzpipe, a data pipeline library. We have three markdown issue templates and people routinely delete the contents before submitting. About 70% of what comes in is bug reports, 20% feature requests, 10% people asking how to use the thing. I want to add a fourth markdown template for support questions so at least those arrive structured. We don't have a forum or a Discord and I'm not starting one. What fields should the support template have?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build a support form, chooser routing deleted from this pass because no destination exists, validated forms promoted to first because bug reports dominate, and a bug form specified field by field with each field justified by the round-trip its absence forces.
expectations: Refuses to create a usage-question issue form and states that usage questions should be routed rather than structured
Deletes chooser routing from this pass because no off-tracker destination exists, rather than listing it as pending or future work
Promotes validated forms to the first intake change because bug reports dominate the inflow at 70%
Replaces the markdown templates with validated forms, stating that markdown templates enforce nothing because the reporter can delete the whole body
Makes the version field a dropdown rather than free text, because free-text versions arrive as "latest"
Requires a minimal reproduction using the project's own APIs rather than a third-party wrapper
Requires logs or output rendered as a code block rather than screenshots of text
Includes a search-first confirmation checkbox
Orders the feature-request fields as problem statement, then proposed solution, then alternatives
Disables blank issues only once the forms cover the real categories
Auto-applies the type label from the form at submission
Justifies each required field by the round-trip its absence forces, and drops fields that do not change the outcome
States the triage minutes each intake change is expected to save

evals.prompt: ashvane, a Kotlin serialization library. Our CONTRIBUTING.md has had a documented triage rota since 2024: six named volunteers, one week each, plus a biweekly triage call. I checked and nobody has actually done a shift since last March, and the call hasn't happened in about that long either. I'm going to re-announce it in the next release notes and remind everyone of their slot. Anything else I should put in the announcement?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to simply re-announce, the dormant-rotation failure named, a two-tier owner-plus-duty design whose mechanics are automated rather than documented, and a liveness check that makes a lapsed shift visible.
expectations: Refuses a plain re-announcement of the existing rota as the fix
Names the failure that documentation still implying coverage is worse than having had no rotation, citing the dormant volunteer triage team precedent
Requires the rota to be retired loudly if it has lapsed, rather than left published while inactive
Designs a two-tier model: a long-term triage owner accountable per component plus a triage duty rotating on a stated shift length
Automates who is on duty rather than what to decide, by syncing the tracker's triage-owner field from a rotation calendar
Names a backup per shift
Adds a liveness check: one metric that would visibly move if the rotation stopped
Sets a stop rule where a session ends at its time box rather than at inbox zero
Sets the session order as newest untriaged first, then items where the reporter replied, then a fixed backlog quota
Grants triage-level permissions for labelling, closing and assigning rather than commit or push access
Defines the escalation rule: what a triager decides alone, what waits for a maintainer, and how long that wait may be
For the recurring call, requires a dedicated queue view, asynchronous pre-triage, and decisions recorded as label or state changes rather than only in minutes
Does not treat writing the rotation down or re-announcing it as the finish line

evals.prompt: nordvex, an OSS analytics collector. Leadership wants me to justify hiring a second triager, so I need numbers. How much contributor retention do we lose per additional day of first response? If we go from 5 days to 3 days, what percentage gain is that? I've also budgeted 3 minutes per issue in the capacity model, that's the standard figure right? And what should I set as our target untriaged percentage so I can put it in the deck.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a per-day retention curve, with the actual evidence described accurately and its limits stated, three minutes labelled as a planning placeholder to be replaced by a timed pilot, and the target figures labelled as starting baselines rather than benchmarks.
expectations: Refuses to supply a per-day retention cost curve and states that no dose-response relationship between triage response time and retention is supported
States that the strongest available evidence measures pull-request first response, not issue triage
Describes that evidence as a binary at-or-under-one-day versus later split rather than a continuous relationship
Notes that the reported deltas are descriptive rather than significance-tested
Reports the newcomer effect as a median of roughly +15 percentage points and the existing-contributor effect as roughly +2 percentage points
Declines to extend the pull-request finding into a general issue-triage service-level promise
Does not supply an invented percentage, curve or benchmark in place of the unsupported figure
Labels three minutes per item as a planning placeholder rather than a standard or measured industry figure
Replaces it by timing a real pilot session and dividing, rather than by importing another constant
Sizes the pilot at roughly 15 to 20 real items and requires it to be run and timed against the new system
Labels the untriaged-share-below-10%, target-met-on-90%, and net-inflow-at-or-below-zero figures as this approach's own starting baselines to be replaced by the project's measured trend
Requires the baseline to be re-run monthly for the first quarter
Recommends lowering the published promise to one the team can hold if the targets do not hold, rather than leaving an unmet number published
